It does not examine household or community water or sanitation service access (c1 = no; Exclusion Criterion 7), the legal/regulatory regime analyzed (WV Code 22-6A-18 baseline water quality testing and oil-and-gas operator presumed pollution liability) regulates extractive-industry contamination damages rather than service-access rules under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification (c2 = no), and the outcome analyzed is emotional distress and epistemic injustice around groundwater quality testing rather than a water or sanitation service access outcome (c4 = no).

Exclude as E04 (Wrong outcome). Although the paper addresses urban household drinking-water reliability in León, Nicaragua, and uses a randomized 2x2 contingent valuation vignette comparing centralized (ENACAL) versus municipal governance, its empirical outcomes are exclusively stated preferences — hypothetical referendum votes / willingness-to-pay (WTP) for a proposed 24/7 service upgrade and attitudinal perceptions of institutional competence — rather than realized water access, connection, service availability, reliability, quantity, affordability, or exclusion (c4 = no). Current daily water supply hours and tap-water expenditures are measured only as baseline covariates within a single city served solely by ENACAL. Furthermore, under the narrow 2026-10-13 reading of Criterion 2, decentralization in León is presented only as a hypothetical survey scenario rather than an operating rule-type mechanism directly governing household service access (plain c2 = yes; narrow c2 = no). Note: statistical non-significance of the provider indicator in the pooled WTP model played no role in this exclusion decision.

Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). Although the paper touches illustratively on rural sanitation (individual toilet construction/coverage) and drinking water administration among 13 developmental sectors managed by two Gram Panchayats in Karnataka, India, the intervention examined is a generic organisational development / internal change-management and capacity-building programme (the GPOD framework: visioning, RACI workflow mapping, informal councillor portfolio management, annual planning, and MIS tracking) aimed at strengthening overall village council efficiency. Per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification, it does not examine a rule-type legal, regulatory, or administrative mechanism directly governing household or community water or sanitation service access, and water/sanitation access is mentioned only as an unquantified illustrative output bullet rather than empirically analysed in relation to any access rule.

This concurrent mixed-methods empirical case study in Jirapa Municipality, northern Ghana satisfies all systematic-review inclusion criteria (c1–c6). It examines household and community drinking-water access, reliability, quantity, rationing, and facility functionality (c1, c4) using primary household survey data (N=225), facility functionality tests (N=118 hand pumps plus piped system), and 15 stakeholder interviews (c3, c5) in English (c6). Although framed broadly around rural and small-town water sustainability alongside technical and seasonal groundwater challenges, it empirically investigates specific rule-type mechanisms under the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 scope: decentralized community ownership and management governance structures (voluntary WSMTs/WATSANs, absence of a constituted Water Management Board required to set tariffs and decide on system expansion and new connections, and Municipal Assembly post-construction support rules) as well as tariff and cost-recovery rules (volumetric domestic and commercial tariffs relative to O&M cost-recovery requirements in Jirapa town and breakdown-only fee collection in rural communities). Per Criterion 6, descriptive quantitative and qualitative socio-legal/institutional evidence without a pooled regression effect estimate remains eligible for systematic-review inclusion.

Excluded under E03 (Wrong exposure). Although the paper empirically describes household/community water coverage and service reliability in Mzuzu City, Malawi (satisfying c1, c3, c4, and c6), it does not examine a rule-type legal, administrative, or regulatory mechanism directly governing service access per the 2026-10-13 Criterion 2 clarification. Instead, it appraises physical infrastructure capacity limits, ESCOM electricity blackouts, technical pipe-network management difficulties in unplanned settlements, and macro utility corporate finances (loan interest burdens, foreign-exchange losses, unaccounted-for water, government institutional arrears, and staffing per 1,000 connections).
